title: the ranges ahead
hook: a hungry hunter waits all night in a tree, and the leaves he drops land somewhere he can't see
carry: do one kind thing without checking

segments.voice: Yesterday, shakti: the goddess, made of every god's light gathered into one, the first ridge of year four. Today, the next ridge.

A hunter has caught nothing all day, and his family is waiting for food. Night comes. He climbs a tree beside a pool, where animals will come to drink, and settles in with his bow. He's cold. He's hungry. He can't let himself sleep. So his hands stay busy: he plucks leaves from the branches and lets them fall, one after another, into the dark below. He has no idea what's down there. The story is told in the Shiva Purana, and retold on one particular night of the year.
screen: `A HUNTER, EMPTY-HANDED.` → `ALL NIGHT IN A TREE.` → `LEAVES FALLING IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Here is the turn, in paraphrase. The tree is a bilva tree, whose leaves are offered to Shiva. And at its foot, unseen in the dark, stands a Shiva linga. All night long, the hunter's restless leaves fall onto it, along with drops of water. He stays awake through every watch of the night. It is Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, though he doesn't know it. When deer come to the water, he draws his bow, and each time he ends up letting them go. By morning, the story says, his heart has changed, and Shiva appears to him. He fasted because he had no food. He kept vigil because he was afraid to sleep. He worshipped because his hands were fidgeting. The story is gentle about it. Shiva accepted the night anyway. That's a fair picture of the second range in year four. After the goddess comes Shiva. The Shiva Purana, in selections. Nataraja, the dancing form, explained piece by piece. The Shiva Sahasranama, a hymn of his names, in selections. The Rudram, a Vedic hymn chanted to him. A first look at Kashmir Shaivism and its Shiva Sutras. And Maha Shivaratri itself, taught as a night-long curriculum, watch by watch, the way the hunter kept it without meaning to. Even from here, some of its forms stand out: the dancer, the ascetic on the mountain, the householder with Parvati, the one who drank poison to save the world.
screen: `A BILVA TREE, A HIDDEN LINGA.` · `A VIGIL KEPT WITHOUT KNOWING.` · `SHIVA ACCEPTS THE NIGHT.` · `THE SECOND RIDGE: SHIVA.` · then, large: `THE DANCER AND THE ASCETIC.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees, as if this were a short watch of the night. Each time you breathe out, picture one leaf leaving your hand and falling into the dark, onto something you can't see, without needing to know where it lands. If you're tired, that's fine; the hunter was too.
Bilva. The tree whose leaves fell, by accident, on a hidden Shiva linga all through the night, the night a hunter kept without knowing it was holy.
Your line: do one kind thing without checking. The hunter never saw where his leaves fell. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, devotees fast, keep vigil through the night, chant to Shiva, and offer water, milk and bilva leaves on the Shiva linga, and the story of the hunter is often retold.

chat.says: The hunter didn't even know it was a holy night. Why did Shiva accept it?
options: The story is gentle: vigil, fast and leaves all counted, even unplanned.
Shiva only accepted it because the hunter confessed everything later.
Because the hunter had secretly been a priest all his life.
chat.meaning: He fasted, kept vigil and offered leaves without meaning to. By morning, the story says, his heart had changed, and Shiva accepted the night.

The hunter story (named Gurudruha in some versions) is told in the Shiva Purana's Koti Rudra Samhita and in other retellings (some put it in the Garuda or Skanda Purana). Versions differ on the deer, the water drops and the ending; the script keeps the common core and says 'the story says'. Please check the chapter reference and the details: bilva tree, hidden linga, water drops, vigil through the watches, deer let go, Shiva appearing.
Shiva Sahasranama is glossed as a hymn of his names, with no count stated.
'The one who drank poison to save the world' refers to Shiva drinking the halahala at the churning of the ocean; confirm the brief phrasing.
